planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Zwartkop aeonium develops its darkest near-black color in bright, cool-season light and greens somewhat in shade or heat.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Zwartkop aeonium develops its darkest near-black color in bright, cool-season light and greens somewhat in shade or heat. Large, glossy rosettes of deep, near-black purple leaves top branching, woody stems on one of the most dramatic and widely recognized dark-foliaged succulents grown, creating striking silhouettes against lighter-colored companions in a mixed succulent bed or container arrangement. Unlike many succulents, aeoniums actively grow through the cooler months and can go semi-dormant or stressed in extreme summer heat, so afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps the plant look its best through summer. Water occasionally through the cooler growing season, reduce watering during the summer semi-dormant period, and propagate easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus before rooting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Kiwi aeonium develops its brightest tricolor pink-and-red edges in bright, cool light.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Kiwi aeonium develops its brightest tricolor pink-and-red edges in bright, cool light. Compact rosettes shift through a striking tricolor pattern of chartreuse-green centers fading to creamy yellow and finishing in a vivid pink-to-red margin, a fruit-like color gradient that gives the cultivar its common name and makes it one of the most colorful small aeoniums commonly grown. Its compact size and vivid, ever-shifting coloring make it a popular choice for succulent arrangements and mixed containers, where its color intensifies in cooler weather and fades somewhat during summer heat and semi-dormancy. Water occasionally through the cooler growing season, reduce watering in summer, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Dinner Plate aeonium forms a flat, single rosette and is monocarpic, dying after flowering once mature.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Dinner Plate aeonium forms a flat, single rosette and is monocarpic, dying after flowering once mature. Hundreds of small, tightly overlapping, fringed leaves arrange themselves into an almost perfectly flat, circular rosette that can reach nearly two feet across, an extraordinary geometric form unlike any other commonly grown succulent, densely covered in fine cilia along the leaf edges that catch the light. Like some other aeoniums it is monocarpic, meaning the rosette flowers once after several years of growth and then dies, so plan to take offsets or start new plants from seed before the parent completes its life cycle. Water occasionally, protect from intense midday sun which can scorch the flat rosette, and grow in a shallow container that showcases its unusual flattened form.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Aeonium decorum branches freely and forms a dense, multi-rosette mound over time.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Aeonium decorum branches freely and forms a dense, multi-rosette mound over time. Small to medium rosettes of pale green leaves edged in fine reddish cilia branch freely from woody stems, quickly forming a dense, bushy mound of dozens of small pinwheel-shaped rosettes, and popular variegated selections add cream and pink striping to the already attractive foliage. Its compact size and freely branching habit make it one of the easier aeoniums to grow into a full, well-shaped specimen relatively quickly compared to slower, less-branching relatives. Water occasionally through the cooler growing season, reduce watering during summer semi-dormancy, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Zebra Wart haworthia tolerates lower light than sun-loving succulents and scorches in direct hot sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Zebra Wart haworthia tolerates lower light than sun-loving succulents and scorches in direct hot sun. Small, dark green, upright, columnar stems are densely covered in raised, pearly white, wart-like tubercles arranged in tidy spiraling rows, an unusual and tactile texture unlike the smooth or striped leaves of most other haworthia species, offsetting readily from the base to form a small clustering colony. Native to South Africa, it tolerates lower light than most succulents, thriving on a bright windowsill without direct sun, making it a good choice for an office or interior space too dim for cacti or echeverias. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright indirect light, and separate offsets to propagate or refresh a crowded pot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Window haworthia spreads by underground rhizomes to form a slowly expanding mat.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Window haworthia spreads by underground rhizomes to form a slowly expanding mat. Fleshy, triangular leaves with translucent, window-like tips arranged in a spiraling rosette allow light to filter down into the leaf tissue, an adaptation shared with several small haworthias native to rocky crevices in southern Africa where much of the plant hides below the soil surface for protection from intense sun. Unlike clustering haworthias that offset from a central rosette, this species spreads by underground rhizomes, sending up new rosettes at a distance from the parent to form a slowly expanding colony over time. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light, and divide the spreading rhizome mat to propagate or share.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Armstrong's gasteria is extremely slow-growing and tolerates low light better than most succulents.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Armstrong's gasteria is extremely slow-growing and tolerates low light better than most succulents. Extremely thick, short, blunt-tipped leaves arranged in two tight, opposite rows give this rare South African miniature an unusually chunky, almost artificial appearance that has earned it the nickname 'concrete aloe' among collectors, growing so slowly that a mature specimen can take many years to reach just a few inches across. Prized among succulent collectors for its unusual, sculptural form and extreme rarity in habitat, it tolerates the lower light of an indoor windowsill better than most succulents, reflecting the shaded rocky crevices it favors in the wild. Water sparingly and only when the soil is completely dry, provide bright but indirect light, and be patient with its exceptionally slow growth rate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Sabre-Leaf gasteria is one of the largest gasteria species and needs a substantial container as it matures.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Sabre-Leaf gasteria is one of the largest gasteria species and needs a substantial container as it matures. Long, curved, sword-like leaves streaked with irregular light and dark green mottling radiate outward in a large, distichous rosette, one of the biggest gasteria species commonly grown, eventually producing tall, arching flower stalks bearing clusters of the characteristic pink-and-green, stomach-shaped flowers that give the genus its name. Native to coastal cliffs in South Africa's Eastern Cape, its considerably larger mature size compared to the many miniature gasteria species makes it a bold specimen for a large container or shaded succulent bed rather than a small windowsill collection. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright indirect light, and give it ample room to reach its substantial mature size.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
